o: Pure simulation: start at index 0 with score 0; 'add' accumulates values[i] and steps forward, 'jump' moves by values[i] (possibly backwards or in place). Stop when leaving the array or hitting an already-executed instruction (that instruction is not re-executed). A boolean visited array detects repeats in O(1).
k: Mark each instruction executed upon arrival, before acting on it.
Termination is guaranteed: each step either exits bounds or marks a new index, and there are only n indices.
values can be negative for jumps, so bounds-check both directions.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear simulation with visited flags
a.i: Follow the pointer mechanically, flipping a visited flag each time we land on an index. The loop condition (in bounds and not visited) encodes both stopping rules exactly as stated.
s: While 0 ≤ i < n and not visited[i]: mark visited[i]; if 'add', add values[i] and i++; else i += values[i].
a.t: O(n) — each index is executed at most once before termination

w: There is essentially one correct approach; the interview value is in translating the termination rules precisely. Pitfalls: executing a revisited instruction a second time (mark visited before processing), off-by-one on the 'jump to i + values[i]' semantics, and using int for the score when n = 1e5 additions of 1e5 can reach 10¹⁰ — use 64-bit. Edge cases: jump of 0 (immediate self-revisit → 0), jump straight out of bounds. Follow-up: what if revisited instructions should execute again up to m times, or if you must detect the cycle entry point?
